intro: Fighting arts have long been taught inside larger institutions. Swedish and German gymnastics halls put fencing beside other exercise. Armies taught boxing to recruits in a few weeks. Colleges built fencing and wrestling teams, and Japanese universities built sumo clubs. Each institution kept what served its goals and set the rest aside.

Schools also faced a question the old masters rarely wrote down: who is responsible when a student is hurt? Courts, lawmakers and sports bodies answered with laws, rulings and new rules. In this unit you will trace those answers with dates and names. You will be able to explain how a school unit, an Army program or a college team changed an art, and why safety rules were rewritten.
bigQuestion: When schools, armies and colleges take in a fighting art, what do they keep, what do they drop, and who writes the rules that protect students?

timeline.t: Emperor Frederick III charters the Marxbrüder fencing guild
Jahn opens the Turnplatz at the Hasenheide in Berlin
Ling founds the Royal Central Institute of Gymnastics in Stockholm
Sargent takes charge of Harvard's Hemenway Gymnasium
Yamashita Yoshitsugu teaches judo to Theodore Roosevelt
Five state associations found the future NFHS in Chicago
The Navy opens four pre-flight schools on college campuses
Illinois passes the Tort Immunity Act
Title IX regulations make most PE classes coeducational
The NCAA rewrites its wrestling weight rules
The U.S. Army publishes FM 3-25.150, Combatives
Washington passes the Lystedt Law on concussions

test.q: Who founded the Royal Central Institute of Gymnastics in 1813?
test.why: Ling founded the Stockholm institute; Jahn worked in Berlin.

test.q: What did Turner clubs press Midwestern school boards to do?
test.why: Turners pushed for gymnastics in public schools and trained early gym teachers.

test.q: What did Sargent do with each Harvard student?
choices: measured the body and wrote an exercise plan
test.why: Sargent used anthropometry to plan each student's exercise.

test.q: Why did the Army teach boxing in 1917 camps?
choices: to build fitness and courage in recruits quickly
test.why: Officers used boxing as fast fitness and morale training.

test.q: Where did Gene Tunney and Jack Dempsey fight in 1927?
test.why: The long count rematch took place at Soldier Field.

test.q: Which arts did the Modern Army Combatives Program draw on?
choices: Brazilian jiu-jitsu, wrestling, boxing, judo and Muay Thai
test.why: Larsen's program borrowed from several arts.

test.q: What does the Title IX PE regulation allow during contact sports?
choices: grouping students by sex inside the class
test.why: Classes stay coeducational, but contact sports may be grouped by sex.

test.q: What did the 1959 Molitor case end in Illinois?
test.why: Molitor ended governmental immunity for school districts.

test.q: Why did the court in Wagenblast refuse school sports waivers?
choices: School sports are a public service and families had little choice
Waivers were written in the wrong language
Only the NCAA can use waivers
test.why: The court said families could not freely refuse, so the waivers failed.

test.q: When did the NCAA first hold a fencing championship?
test.why: Men's NCAA fencing began in 1941; women's in 1982.

test.q: What was the Midwest Federation formed in Chicago in 1920?
choices: the group that became the NFHS
test.why: It grew into the National Federation of State High School Associations.

test.q: Who taught judo at the U.S. Naval Academy around 1905?
test.why: Yamashita, a Kodokan teacher, taught there after teaching Roosevelt.

test.q: What rank did Wajima reach in 1973?
test.why: Wajima became yokozuna, the top rank in professional sumo.

test.q: What did the 1998 NCAA weight rules ban?
choices: rubber suits and saunas for losing weight
test.why: The rules banned practices tied to the 1997 deaths.

test.q: Which three parts did the Lystedt Law require?
choices: education, removal from play, and written clearance to return
test.why: The law requires concussion education, removal and clearance by a licensed provider.

write.prompt: Did schools and colleges change fighting arts more to fit their goals or to protect students? Argue using at least three dated records from the unit, such as Ling's 1813 institute, the 1975 Title IX PE regulation, the 1998 NCAA weight rules or the 2009 Lystedt Law.
tips: Name each record and its year, such as Wagenblast v. Odessa School District, 1988.
Say which institution made each change: a state, a court, the NCAA or an army.
Compare what the art looked like before and after the institution took it in.
Use unit terms like combatives, coeducational, tort and eligibility.
Attribute beliefs about safety to the people or bodies who held them.
